claim: Slo2 potassium channels play important roles in neuronal function.
source: Slo2 potassium channels play important roles in neuronal function, and their mutations in humans may cause epilepsies and cognitive defects.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the broader scientific literature on Slo2 channels.

claim: Mutations of Slo2 channels in humans may cause epilepsies and cognitive defects.
source: Slo2 potassium channels play important roles in neuronal function, and their mutations in humans may cause epilepsies and cognitive defects.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The function of C. elegans Slo2 (SLO-2) depends on adr-1.
source: Here we show that the function of C. elegans Slo2 (SLO-2) depends on adr-1, a gene important to RNA editing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that adr-1 mutants suppress SLO-2 gain-of-function phenotypes and reduce SLO-2 currents.

claim: adr-1 is a gene important to RNA editing.
source: Here we show that the function of C. elegans Slo2 (SLO-2) depends on adr-1, a gene important to RNA editing.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about ADR-1's role in RNA editing.

claim: ADR-1 promotes SLO-2 function not by editing the transcripts of slo-2 but those of scyl-1.
source: ADR-1 promotes SLO-2 function not by editing the transcripts of slo-2 but those of scyl-1, which encodes an orthologue of mammalian SCYL1.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing no editing in slo-2 transcripts but editing in scyl-1 transcripts.

claim: scyl-1 encodes an orthologue of mammalian SCYL1.
source: ADR-1 promotes SLO-2 function not by editing the transcripts of slo-2 but those of scyl-1, which encodes an orthologue of mammalian SCYL1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence homology analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transcripts of scyl-1 are greatly decreased in adr-1 mutants due to deficient RNA editing at a single adenosine in their 3'-UTR.
source: Transcripts of scyl-1 are greatly decreased in adr-1 mutants due to deficient RNA editing at a single adenosine in their 3'-UTR.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and reporter assays showing reduced scyl-1 expression in adr-1 mutants.

claim: SCYL-1 physically interacts with SLO-2 in neurons.
source: SCYL-1 physically interacts with SLO-2 in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Single-channel open probability (Po) of neuronal SLO-2 is ~50% lower in scyl-1 knockout mutant than wild type.
source: Single-channel open probability (Po) of neuronal SLO-2 is ~50% lower in scyl-1 knockout mutant than wild type.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel patch-clamp recordings from VA5 motor neurons.

claim: Human Slo2.2/Slack Po is doubled by SCYL1 in a heterologous expression system.
source: Moreover, human Slo2.2/Slack Po is doubled by SCYL1 in a heterologous expression system.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recordings from Xenopus oocytes expressing human Slo2.2 with or without SCYL1.

claim: SCYL-1/SCYL1 is an evolutionarily conserved regulator of Slo2 channels.
source: These results suggest that SCYL-1/SCYL1 is an evolutionarily conserved regulator of Slo2 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects of SCYL-1 on C. elegans SLO-2 and SCYL1 on human Slo2.2.

claim: Slo2 channels are large-conductance potassium channels existing in mammals as well as invertebrates.
source: Slo2 channels are large-conductance potassium channels existing in mammals as well as invertebrates (Kaczmarek, 2013; Yuan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Slo2 channels are the primary conductor of delayed outward currents in many neurons examined.
source: They are the primary conductor of delayed outward currents in many neurons examined (Budelli et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human and mouse each has two Slo2 channels (Slo2.1/Slick and Slo2.2/Slack).
source: Human and mouse each has two Slo2 channels (Slo2.1/Slick and Slo2.2/Slack) (Kaczmarek, 2013), whereas the nematode C. elegans has only one (SLO-2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The nematode C. elegans has only one Slo2 channel (SLO-2).
source: Human and mouse each has two Slo2 channels (Slo2.1/Slick and Slo2.2/Slack) (Kaczmarek, 2013), whereas the nematode C. elegans has only one (SLO-2).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about C. elegans genetics.

claim: Slo2 channels are abundantly expressed in the nervous system.
source: These channels are abundantly expressed in the nervous system (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002; Bhattacharjee et al., 2005; Joiner et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2018; Rizzi et al., 2016), and play major roles in shaping neuronal electrical properties and regulating neurotransmitter release (Kaczmarek, 2013; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Slo2 channels play major roles in shaping neuronal electrical properties and regulating neurotransmitter release.
source: These channels are abundantly expressed in the nervous system (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002; Bhattacharjee et al., 2005; Joiner et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2018; Rizzi et al., 2016), and play major roles in shaping neuronal electrical properties and regulating neurotransmitter release (Kaczmarek, 2013; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations of Slo2 channels cause epilepsies and severe intellectual disabilities in humans.
source: Mutations of Slo2 channels cause epilepsies and severe intellectual disabilities in humans (Ambrosino et al., 2018; Cataldi et al., 2019; Evely et al., 2017; Gururaj et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2017; Kawasaki et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2016; McTague et al., 2018; Rizzo et al., 2016), and reduced tolerance to hypoxic environment in worms (Yuan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Mutations of Slo2 channels cause reduced tolerance to hypoxic environment in worms.
source: Mutations of Slo2 channels cause epilepsies and severe intellectual disabilities in humans (Ambrosino et al., 2018; Cataldi et al., 2019; Evely et al., 2017; Gururaj et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2017; Kawasaki et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2016; McTague et al., 2018; Rizzo et al., 2016), and reduced tolerance to hypoxic environment in worms (Yuan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Physiological functions of Slo2 channels depend on other proteins.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that physiological functions of these channels depend on other proteins.
evidence: This is supported by examples provided in the text with citations.

claim: In mice, the fragile mental retardation protein (FMRP), a RNA binding protein, enhances Slack activity by binding to its carboxyl terminus.
source: For example, in mice, the fragile mental retardation protein (FMRP), a RNA binding protein, enhances Slack activity by binding to its carboxyl terminus (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In worms, HRPU-2, a RNA/DNA binding protein, controls the expression level of SLO-2 through a posttranscriptional effect.
source: In worms, HRPU-2, a RNA/DNA binding protein, controls the expression level of SLO-2 through a posttranscriptional effect (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: RNA editing is an evolutionally conserved post-transcriptional process catalyzed by ADARs (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA).
source: RNA editing is an evolutionally conserved post-transcriptional process catalyzed by ADARs (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA) (Gott and Emeson, 2000; Jin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ADARs convert adenosine (A) to inosine (I) in double-stranded RNA.
source: ADARs convert adenosine (A) to inosine (I) in double-stranded RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR function.

claim: Inosine is interpreted as guanosine (G) by cellular machineries.
source: Since inosine is interpreted as guanosine (G) by cellular machineries (Basilio et al., 1962), A-to-I RNA editing may alter the function of a protein by changing its coding potential, or regulate gene expression through altering alternative splicing, microRNA processing, or RNA interference (Deffit and Hundley, 2016; Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A-to-I RNA editing may alter the function of a protein by changing its coding potential.
source: Since inosine is interpreted as guanosine (G) by cellular machineries (Basilio et al., 1962), A-to-I RNA editing may alter the function of a protein by changing its coding potential, or regulate gene expression through altering alternative splicing, microRNA processing, or RNA interference (Deffit and Hundley, 2016; Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A-to-I RNA editing may regulate gene expression through altering alternative splicing, microRNA processing, or RNA interference.
source: Since inosine is interpreted as guanosine (G) by cellular machineries (Basilio et al., 1962), A-to-I RNA editing may alter the function of a protein by changing its coding potential, or regulate gene expression through altering alternative splicing, microRNA processing, or RNA interference (Deffit and Hundley, 2016; Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human and mouse each has three ADARs: ADAR1, ADAR2 and ADAR3.
source: Human and mouse each has three ADARs: ADAR1, ADAR2 and ADAR3 (Chen et al., 2000; Kim et al., 1994; Melcher et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ADAR1 and ADAR2 possess deaminase activity and catalyze the A-to-I conversion.
source: ADAR1 and ADAR2 possess deaminase activity and catalyze the A-to-I conversion (Tan et al., 2017), whereas ADAR3 is catalytically inactive with regulatory roles in RNA editing (Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ADAR3 is catalytically inactive with regulatory roles in RNA editing.
source: ADAR1 and ADAR2 possess deaminase activity and catalyze the A-to-I conversion (Tan et al., 2017), whereas ADAR3 is catalytically inactive with regulatory roles in RNA editing (Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Millions of A-to-I editing sites have been detected in the human transcriptome through RNA-seq.
source: Millions of A-to-I editing sites have been detected in the human transcriptome through RNA-seq, with the vast majority of them found in non-coding regions (Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The vast majority of A-to-I editing sites in the human transcriptome are found in non-coding regions.
source: Millions of A-to-I editing sites have been detected in the human transcriptome through RNA-seq, with the vast majority of them found in non-coding regions (Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Little is known about the roles of RNA editing in non-coding regions.
source: However, little is known about the roles of RNA editing in non-coding regions (Nishikura, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: adr-1 encodes one of two ADARs in C. elegans (ADR-1 and ADR-2).
source: In a genetic screen for suppressors of a sluggish phenotype caused by expressing a hyperactive SLO-2 in worms, we isolated mutants of several genes, including adr-1, which encodes one of two ADARs in C. elegans (ADR-1 and ADR-2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans genetics.

claim: ADR-2 has deaminase activity and plays an indispensable role in the A-to-I conversion.
source: While ADR-2 has deaminase activity and plays an indispensable role in the A-to-I conversion, ADR-1 is catalytically inactive but can promote RNA editing by binding to selected target mRNA and tethering ADR-2 to RNA substrates (Ganem et al., 2019; Rajendren et al., 2018; Washburn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ADR-1 is catalytically inactive but can promote RNA editing by binding to selected target mRNA and tethering ADR-2 to RNA substrates.
source: While ADR-2 has deaminase activity and plays an indispensable role in the A-to-I conversion, ADR-1 is catalytically inactive but can promote RNA editing by binding to selected target mRNA and tethering ADR-2 to RNA substrates (Ganem et al., 2019; Rajendren et al., 2018; Washburn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of adr-1 inhibit SLO-2 function through impairing RNA editing of scyl-1.
source: We found that loss-of-function (lf) mutations of adr-1 inhibit SLO-2 function through impairing RNA editing of scyl-1, which encodes an orthologue of human and mouse SCYL1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced scyl-1 expression and deficient RNA editing in adr-1 mutants.

claim: In adr-1(lf) mutants, a lack of A-to-I conversion at a specific site in scyl-1 3'-UTR causes reduced scyl-1 expression.
source: In adr-1(lf) mutants, a lack of A-to-I conversion at a specific site in scyl-1 3'-UTR causes reduced scyl-1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and reporter assays.

claim: Knockout of scyl-1 severely reduces SLO-2 current in worms.
source: Knockout of scyl-1 severely reduces SLO-2 current in worms whereas coexpression of SCYL1 with human Slack in Xenopus oocytes greatly augments channel activity.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell current recordings from motor neurons.

claim: Coexpression of SCYL1 with human Slack in Xenopus oocytes greatly augments channel activity.
source: Knockout of scyl-1 severely reduces SLO-2 current in worms whereas coexpression of SCYL1 with human Slack in Xenopus oocytes greatly augments channel activity.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recordings from Xenopus oocytes.

claim: SCYL-1/SCYL1 proteins likely play an evolutionarily conserved role in physiological functions of Slo2 channels.
source: These results suggest that SCYL-1/SCYL1 proteins likely play an evolutionarily conserved role in physiological functions of Slo2 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects of SCYL-1 and SCYL1 on Slo2 channels in different species.

claim: Mutations or knockout of mammalian SCYL1 may cause neural degeneration, intellectual disabilities, and liver failure.
source: Mutations or knockout mammalian SCYL1 may cause neural degeneration, intellectual disabilities, and liver failure, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear (Lenz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Shohet et al., 2019; Spagnoli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical and animal studies.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of SCYL1 mutation-associated diseases are unclear.
source: Mutations or knockout mammalian SCYL1 may cause neural degeneration, intellectual disabilities, and liver failure, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear (Lenz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Shohet et al., 2019; Spagnoli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The revelation of SCYL-1/SCYL1 as a protein important to Slo2 channels suggests a potential link between diseases caused by SCLY1 mutations and Slo2 channel functions.
source: The revelation of SCYL-1/SCYL1 as a protein important to Slo2 channels suggests a potential link between diseases caused by SCLY1 mutations and Slo2 channel functions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: zw80 and zw81 carry nonsense mutations leading to premature stops at tryptophan (W) 366 and W33, respectively.
source: zw80 and zw81 carry nonsense mutations leading to premature stops at tryptophan (W) 366 and W33, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: slo-2(gf) worms showed greatly decreased locomotion speed compared with wild type.
source: slo-2(gf) worms showed greatly decreased locomotion speed compared with wild type, and this phenotype was substantially alleviated in slo-2(gf);adr-1(lf) double mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) was substantially alleviated in slo-2(gf);adr-1(lf) double mutants.
source: slo-2(gf) worms showed greatly decreased locomotion speed compared with wild type, and this phenotype was substantially alleviated in slo-2(gf);adr-1(lf) double mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A new adr-1 mutant allele (zw96) was created by introducing a premature stop codon at serine (S) 333 using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach.
source: To confirm that the suppression of slo-2(gf) phenotype resulted from mutations of adr-1 rather than that of another gene, we created a new adr-1 mutant allele (zw96) by introducing a premature stop codon at serine (S) 333 (Figure 1A) using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach.
evidence: This is supported by the methods used to generate the mutant and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) was similarly suppressed by adr-1(zw96).
source: The sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) was similarly suppressed by adr-1(zw96), which, by itself, did not enhance locomotion speed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: adr-1(zw96), by itself, did not enhance locomotion speed.
source: The sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) was similarly suppressed by adr-1(zw96), which, by itself, did not enhance locomotion speed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of wild-type adr-1 under the control of the pan-neuronal rab-3 promotor (Prab-3) in slo-2(gf);adr-1(zw96) unmasked the sluggish phenotype.
source: Expression of wild-type adr-1 under the control of the pan-neuronal rab-3 promotor (Prab-3) in slo-2(gf);adr-1(zw96) unmasked the sluggish phenotype (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) is mainly caused by SLO-2 hyperactivity in neurons.
source: These results indicate that the sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) is mainly caused by SLO-2 hyperactivity in neurons, and that neuronal function of SLO-2(gf) depends on ADR-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that neuronal expression of adr-1 restores the sluggish phenotype.

claim: Neuronal function of SLO-2(gf) depends on ADR-1.
source: These results indicate that the sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) is mainly caused by SLO-2 hyperactivity in neurons, and that neuronal function of SLO-2(gf) depends on ADR-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and rescue experiments.

claim: In C. elegans, cholinergic motor neurons control body-wall muscle cells by producing bursts of postsynaptic currents (PSC bursts).
source: In C. elegans, cholinergic motor neurons control body-wall muscle cells by producing bursts of postsynaptic currents (PSC bursts) (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Compared with wild type, the slo-2(gf) strain displayed much larger outward currents.
source: Compared with wild type, the slo-2(gf) strain displayed much larger outward currents, and greatly decreased PSC burst frequency, duration and charge transfer (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: The slo-2(gf) strain showed greatly decreased PSC burst frequency, duration and charge transfer compared with wild type.
source: Compared with wild type, the slo-2(gf) strain displayed much larger outward currents, and greatly decreased PSC burst frequency, duration and charge transfer (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: These phenotypes of slo-2(gf) were mostly suppressed in the slo-2(gf);adr-1(zw96) strain.
source: These phenotypes of slo-2(gf) were mostly suppressed in the slo-2(gf);adr-1(zw96) strain (Figure 1C and D), suggesting that adr-1(lf) alleviated the sluggish phenotype through inhibiting SLO-2(gf).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: adr-1(lf) alleviated the sluggish phenotype through inhibiting SLO-2(gf).
source: These phenotypes of slo-2(gf) were mostly suppressed in the slo-2(gf);adr-1(zw96) strain (Figure 1C and D), suggesting that adr-1(lf) alleviated the sluggish phenotype through inhibiting SLO-2(gf).
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Expression of wild-type adr-1 in neurons of slo-2(gf);adr-1(zw96) unmasked the effects of slo-2(gf) on VA5 whole-cell currents and PSC bursts.
source: In addition, expression of wild-type adr-1 in neurons of slo-2(gf);adr-1(zw96) unmasked the effects of slo-2(gf) on VA5 whole-cell currents and PSC bursts (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: The suppressing effect of adr-1(lf) on the slo-2(gf) sluggish phenotype was likely due to reduced SLO-2 activities in motor neurons.
source: These observations suggest that the suppressing effect of adr-1(lf) on the slo-2(gf) sluggish phenotype was likely due to reduced SLO-2 activities in motor neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: ADR-2 is required for RNA editing.
source: We suspected that the suppression of SLO-2(gf) by adr-1(lf) resulted from deficient RNA-editing. If so, adr-2(lf) might also suppress the sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) because ADR-2 is required for RNA editing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADR-2 function.

claim: The sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) worms was substantially alleviated in slo-2(gf);adr-2(lf) double mutants.
source: Indeed, the sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) worms was substantially alleviated in slo-2(gf);adr-2(lf) double mutants (Figure 2A), and the augmenting effect of slo-2(gf) on VA5 whole-cell outward currents was mostly eliminated by adr-2(lf) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion tracking data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The augmenting effect of slo-2(gf) on VA5 whole-cell outward currents was mostly eliminated by adr-2(lf).
source: Indeed, the sluggish phenotype of slo-2(gf) worms was substantially alleviated in slo-2(gf);adr-2(lf) double mutants (Figure 2A), and the augmenting effect of slo-2(gf) on VA5 whole-cell outward currents was mostly eliminated by adr-2(lf) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: adr-2(lf) brought VA5 whole-cell currents below the wild-type level.
source: Furthermore, adr-2(lf) brought VA5 whole-cell currents below the wild-type level (Figure 2B), which presumably resulted from reduced activities of wild-type SLO-2.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The reduction of VA5 whole-cell currents below wild-type level in adr-2(lf) presumably resulted from reduced activities of wild-type SLO-2.
source: Furthermore, adr-2(lf) brought VA5 whole-cell currents below the wild-type level (Figure 2B), which presumably resulted from reduced activities of wild-type SLO-2.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data.

claim: RNA editing is important to SLO-2 function in neurons.
source: These results suggest that RNA editing is important to SLO-2 function in neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of adr-2 mutations on SLO-2 currents.

claim: Strong GFP expression was observed in the nervous system of transgenic worms expressing GFP under the control of adr-1 promoter.
source: In transgenic worms, strong GFP expression was observed in the nervous system, including ventral cord motor neurons and many neurons in the head and tail, while weak GFP expression was observed in the intestine and body-wall muscles (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Weak GFP expression was observed in the intestine and body-wall muscles of transgenic worms expressing GFP under the control of adr-1 promoter.
source: In transgenic worms, strong GFP expression was observed in the nervous system, including ventral cord motor neurons and many neurons in the head and tail, while weak GFP expression was observed in the intestine and body-wall muscles (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ADR-1::GFP is localized in the nucleus.
source: We found that ADR-1::GFP is localized in the nucleus, as indicated by its colocalization with the mStrawberry-tagged nucleus marker HIS-58 (Liu et al., 2018) in ventral cord motor neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging showing colocalization with a nuclear marker in Figure 3B.

claim: The expression patterns of adr-1 and slo-2 overlapped extensively in the nervous system.
source: We found that the expression patterns of adr-1 and slo-2 overlapped extensively in the nervous system (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The majority of ventral cord motor neurons and numerous head neurons were colabeled by GFP and mStrawberry in worms expressing Padr-1::GFP and Pslo-2::mStrawberry.
source: For example, the majority of ventral cord motor neurons and numerous head neurons were colabeled by GFP and mStrawberry (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SLO-2 is the primary conductor of delayed outward currents in C. elegans cholinergic motor neurons.
source: SLO-2 is the primary conductor of delayed outward currents in C. elegans cholinergic motor neurons (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: VA5 delayed outward currents were dramatically smaller in slo-2(lf) than wild type.
source: Consistent with our previous report (Liu et al., 2014), VA5 delayed outward currents were dramatically smaller and VA5 resting membrane potential was much less hyperpolarized in slo-2(lf) than wild type.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: VA5 resting membrane potential was much less hyperpolarized in slo-2(lf) than wild type.
source: Consistent with our previous report (Liu et al., 2014), VA5 delayed outward currents were dramatically smaller and VA5 resting membrane potential was much less hyperpolarized in slo-2(lf) than wild type.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: adr-1(lf) caused significantly decreased outward currents and less hyperpolarized resting membrane potential in VA5.
source: While adr-1(lf) also caused significantly decreased outward currents and less hyperpolarized resting membrane potential in VA5, it did not produce additive effects when combined with slo-2(lf) (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: adr-1(lf) did not produce additive effects when combined with slo-2(lf) on VA5 outward currents and resting membrane potential.
source: While adr-1(lf) also caused significantly decreased outward currents and less hyperpolarized resting membrane potential in VA5, it did not produce additive effects when combined with slo-2(lf) (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: adr-1(lf) affects motor neuron outward currents and resting membrane potential through SLO-2.
source: These results suggest that adr-1(lf) affects motor neuron outward currents and resting membrane potential through SLO-2.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effects in double mutants.

claim: adr-1(lf) caused an increase in the duration and mean charge transfer rate of PSC bursts without altering the burst frequency compared with wild type.
source: We found that adr-1(lf) caused an increase in the duration and mean charge transfer rate of PSC bursts without altering the burst frequency compared with wild type (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 4D and E.

claim: These phenotypes of adr-1(lf) were similar to those of slo-2(lf) and did not become more severe in the double mutants.
source: These phenotypes of adr-1(lf) were similar to those of slo-2(lf) and did not become more severe in the double mutants (Figure 4D and E), suggesting that ADR-1 modulates neurotransmitter release through SLO-2.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 4D and E.

claim: ADR-1 modulates neurotransmitter release through SLO-2.
source: These phenotypes of adr-1(lf) were similar to those of slo-2(lf) and did not become more severe in the double mutants (Figure 4D and E), suggesting that ADR-1 modulates neurotransmitter release through SLO-2.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effects in double mutants.

claim: No RNA editing event was detected in slo-2 transcripts.
source: Unexpectedly, no RNA editing event was detected in slo-2 transcripts, and slo-2 mRNA level was similar between wild type and the adr-1 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: slo-2 mRNA level was similar between wild type and the adr-1 mutant.
source: Unexpectedly, no RNA editing event was detected in slo-2 transcripts, and slo-2 mRNA level was similar between wild type and the adr-1 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ADR-1 might regulate SLO-2 function through RNA editing of another gene.
source: These results suggest that ADR-1 might regulate SLO-2 function through RNA editing of another gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of editing in slo-2 transcripts.

claim: A previous study identified 270 high-confidence editing sites in transcripts of 51 genes expressed in C. elegans neurons.
source: A previous study identified 270 high-confidence editing sites in transcripts of 51 genes expressed in C. elegans neurons (Washburn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Two genes, rncs-1 and scyl-1, were reduced greatly in adr-1(lf) compared with wild type.
source: Most of these genes showed either no decrease or only a small decrease in expression, but two of these genes, rncs-1 and scyl-1, were reduced greatly in adr-1(lf) compared with wild type (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: rncs-1 is a non-coding gene expressed in the hypodermis and vulva.
source: rncs-1 is not a conceivable candidate for the putative SLO-2 regulator because it is a non-coding gene expressed in the hypodermis and vulva (Hellwig and Bass, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SCYL-1 has an amino-terminal kinase domain that lacks residues critical to kinase activity.
source: Like its mammalian homologs, SCYL-1 has an amino-terminal kinase domain that lacks residues critical to kinase activity, and a central domain containing five HEAT repeats (HEAT for Huntingtin, elongation factor 3, protein phosphatase 2A, yeast kinase TOR1) (Pelletier, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review and sequence analysis.

claim: SCYL-1 has a central domain containing five HEAT repeats.
source: Like its mammalian homologs, SCYL-1 has an amino-terminal kinase domain that lacks residues critical to kinase activity, and a central domain containing five HEAT repeats (HEAT for Huntingtin, elongation factor 3, protein phosphatase 2A, yeast kinase TOR1) (Pelletier, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review and sequence analysis.

claim: SCYL-1 shares 38% identity and 60% similarity with human SCYL1.
source: SCYL-1 shares 38% identity and 60% similarity with human SCYL1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The HEAT domain shows a very high level of sequence homology (53% identity and 76% similarity) between SCYL-1 and human SCYL1.
source: Notably, amino acid sequence in the HEAT domain, which is often highly degenerative (Pelletier, 2016), shows a very high level of sequence homology (53% identity and 76% similarity) between these two proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-expression of scyl-1 and slo-2 was observed in many ventral cord motor neurons.
source: Co-expression of scyl-1 and slo-2 was observed in many ventral cord motor neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most other neurons expressing slo-2 did not appear to express scyl-1.
source: However, most other neurons expressing slo-2 (e. g. head and tail neurons) did not appear to express scyl-1.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging.

claim: scyl-1 expression was detected in some cells that did not express slo-2, including the excretory cell, spermatheca, uterine ventral cells, and intestinal cells.
source: In addition, scyl-1 expression was detected in some cells that did not express slo-2, including the excretory cell, spermatheca, uterine ventral cells, and intestinal cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6.

claim: scyl-1(zw99) showed a substantial decrease in VA5 outward currents compared with wild type.
source: scyl-1(zw99) showed a substantial decrease in VA5 outward currents compared with wild type; this phenotype could be rescued by expressing wild-type SCYL-1 in neurons, and was non-additive with that of either slo-2(lf) or adr-1(zw96) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The phenotype of scyl-1(zw99) could be rescued by expressing wild-type SCYL-1 in neurons.
source: scyl-1(zw99) showed a substantial decrease in VA5 outward currents compared with wild type; this phenotype could be rescued by expressing wild-type SCYL-1 in neurons, and was non-additive with that of either slo-2(lf) or adr-1(zw96) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The phenotype of scyl-1(zw99) was non-additive with that of either slo-2(lf) or adr-1(zw96).
source: scyl-1(zw99) showed a substantial decrease in VA5 outward currents compared with wild type; this phenotype could be rescued by expressing wild-type SCYL-1 in neurons, and was non-additive with that of either slo-2(lf) or adr-1(zw96) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SCYL-1 and ADR-1 likely act in a common pathway to contribute to SLO-2 function.
source: These results suggest that SCYL-1 and ADR-1 likely act in a common pathway to contribute to SLO-2 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-additive effects of the mutations.

claim: GFP signal in the ventral nerve cord was similar between wild type and the scyl-1 mutant expressing Prab-3::SLO-2::GFP.
source: We found that GFP signal in the ventral nerve cord was similar between wild type and the scyl-1 mutant (Figure 7B), suggesting that SCYL-1 does not regulate SLO-2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SCYL-1 does not regulate SLO-2 expression.
source: We found that GFP signal in the ventral nerve cord was similar between wild type and the scyl-1 mutant (Figure 7B), suggesting that SCYL-1 does not regulate SLO-2 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar GFP signal in wild type and mutant.

claim: SLO-2 showed >50% decrease in open probability (Po) without a change of single-channel conductance in scyl-1(zw99) compared with wild type.
source: SLO-2 showed >50% decrease in open probability (Po) without a change of single-channel conductance in scyl-1(zw99) compared with wild type, and this mutant phenotype was completely rescued by neuronal expression of wild-type SCYL-1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recordings shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The mutant phenotype of scyl-1(zw99) was completely rescued by neuronal expression of wild-type SCYL-1.
source: SLO-2 showed >50% decrease in open probability (Po) without a change of single-channel conductance in scyl-1(zw99) compared with wild type, and this mutant phenotype was completely rescued by neuronal expression of wild-type SCYL-1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recordings shown in Figure 8A.

claim: SLO-2 has at least two open states and three closed states.
source: Analyses of single-channel open and closed events revealed that SLO-2 has at least two open states and three closed states, and that the decreased Po of SLO-2 in scyl-1(lf) mainly resulted from shorter and fewer long openings (Figure 8B) and a larger proportion of the longest closings (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by dwell time analysis shown in Figures 8B and C.

claim: The decreased Po of SLO-2 in scyl-1(lf) mainly resulted from shorter and fewer long openings and a larger proportion of the longest closings.
source: Analyses of single-channel open and closed events revealed that SLO-2 has at least two open states and three closed states, and that the decreased Po of SLO-2 in scyl-1(lf) mainly resulted from shorter and fewer long openings (Figure 8B) and a larger proportion of the longest closings (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by dwell time analysis shown in Figures 8B and C.

claim: YFP fluorescence was observed in ventral cord motor neurons when either the full-length or the C-terminal of SLO-2 was used but not when the N-terminal was used in the BiFC assays.
source: We observed YFP fluorescence in ventral cord motor neurons when either the full-length or the C-terminal of SLO-2 was used but not when the N-terminal was used in the assays (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay results shown in Figure 9B.

claim: SCYL-1 immunoprecipitated with either full-length SLO-2 or SLO-2 C-terminal but not SLO-2 N-terminal.
source: We found that the SCYL-1 immunoprecipitated with either full-length SLO-2 or SLO-2 C-terminal but not SLO-2 N-terminal (Figure 9C), which is in agreement with the BiFC results.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation results shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Both the BiFC and coimmunoprecipitation results suggest that SCYL-1 physically interacts with SLO-2, and this interaction is mediated by SLO-2 carboxyl terminal.
source: Thus, both the BiFC and coimmunoprecipitation results suggest that SCYL-1 physically interacts with SLO-2, and this interaction is mediated by SLO-2 carboxyl terminal.
evidence: This is inferred from the BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: RNA-Seq data revealed eight high-frequency (>15%) adenosine-to-guanosine editing sites in scyl-1 transcripts of wild type.
source: Our RNA-Seq data revealed eight high-frequency (>15%) adenosine-to-guanosine editing sites in scyl-1 transcripts of wild type (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: All these editing sites are located within a predicted 746 bp hair-pin structure in the 3' end of scyl-1 pre-mRNA.
source: All these editing sites are located within a predicted 746 bp hair-pin structure in the 3' end of scyl-1 pre-mRNA, which contains an inverted repeat with >98% complementary base pairing (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction shown in Figure 10B.

claim: RNA editing at only one of these sites was significantly deficient (by 74%) in adr-1(zw96) compared with wild type.
source: Interestingly, RNA editing at only one of these sites was significantly deficient (by 74%) in adr-1(zw96) compared with wild type (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: RNA editing at the ADR-1-dependent site was deficient in both the adr-1 and adr-2 mutants.
source: Sanger sequencing of scyl-1 mRNA and the corresponding genomic DNA from wild type, adr-1(zw96), and adr-2(gv42) showed that RNA editing at this site was deficient in both the adr-1 and adr-2 mutants whereas that at an adjacent site was deficient only in the adr-2 mutant (Figure 10C), suggesting that RNA editing at the site impaired by adr-1(lf) might be important to scyl-1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing results shown in Figure 10C.

claim: RNA editing at an adjacent site was deficient only in the adr-2 mutant.
source: Sanger sequencing of scyl-1 mRNA and the corresponding genomic DNA from wild type, adr-1(zw96), and adr-2(gv42) showed that RNA editing at this site was deficient in both the adr-1 and adr-2 mutants whereas that at an adjacent site was deficient only in the adr-2 mutant (Figure 10C), suggesting that RNA editing at the site impaired by adr-1(lf) might be important to scyl-1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing results shown in Figure 10C.

claim: GFP signal was observed in worms harboring wp1924 but no GFP signal was detected in worms harboring wp1923.
source: GFP signal was observed in worms harboring wp1924 but no GFP signal was detected in worms harboring wp1923 (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 10E.

claim: GFP signal was ~50% weaker in the adr-1(zw96) mutant than wild type expressing the wp1924 transgene.
source: GFP signal was ~50% weaker in the mutant than wild type (Figure 10F and G).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figures 10F and G.

claim: ADR-1 can also increase scyl-1 mRNA level through a post-editing effect.
source: Because the transgene mimicked the edited 3'-UTR sequence of scyl-1 mRNA, the weaker GFP signal in the mutant than wild type suggests that ADR-1 can also increase scyl-1 mRNA level through a post-editing effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter assay results.

claim: Eleven mutants with reduced GFP expression were isolated from ~5000 mutagenized haploid genomes in a pilot genetic screen.
source: Indeed, eleven mutants with reduced GFP expression were isolated from ~5000 mutagenized haploid genomes in a pilot genetic screen, as shown by two examples (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic screen results shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The deficiency of GFP expression in these mutants was related to the function of scyl-1 3'-UTR.
source: The deficiency of GFP expression in these mutants was related to the function of scyl-1 3'-UTR because GFP expression from a control transgene with unc-10 3'-UTR was not compromised in these mutants (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the control experiment shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: SCYL1 increased hSlo2.2 Po greatly without altering the single-channel conductance.
source: SCYL1 increased hSlo2.2 Po greatly without altering the single-channel conductance (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recordings from Xenopus oocytes shown in Figure 11A.

claim: hSlo2.2 has at least two open states and three closed states.
source: The channel has at least two open states and three closed states (Figure 11B–D).
evidence: This is supported by dwell time analysis shown in Figures 11B-D.

claim: SCYL1 increased hSlo2.2 Po mainly by increasing the duration and proportion of the longer open state, and shortening the duration of the longest closed state.
source: Dwell time analyses indicate that SCYL1 increased hSlo2.2 Po mainly by increasing the duration and proportion of the longer open state, and shortening the duration of the longest closed state (Figure 11B–D).
evidence: This is supported by dwell time analysis shown in Figures 11B-D.

claim: The overall effect of SCYL1 on hSlo2.2 Po is similar to that of SCYL-1 on SLO-2 Po in wild-type worms.
source: The overall effect of SCYL1 on hSlo2.2 Po is similar to that of SCYL-1 on SLO-2 Po in wild-type worms (Figure 8).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the effects in different systems.

claim: A physiological function of both mammalian SCYL1 and worm SCYL-1 is to enhance Slo2 channel activities.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that a physiological function of both mammalian SCYL1 and worm SCYL-1 is to enhance Slo2 channel activities.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in both C. elegans and Xenopus oocytes.

claim: Both ADR-1 and SCYL-1 are critical to SLO-2 physiological function in neurons.
source: This study shows that both ADR-1 and SCYL-1 are critical to SLO-2 physiological function in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: ADR-1 enhances SLO-2 function indirectly through promoting SCYL-1 expression.
source: While ADR-1 enhances SLO-2 function indirectly through promoting SCYL-1 expression, SCYL-1 regulates SLO-2 through physical interactions.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data, reporter assays, and the lack of direct editing of slo-2 transcripts.

claim: SCYL-1 regulates SLO-2 through physical interactions.
source: While ADR-1 enhances SLO-2 function indirectly through promoting SCYL-1 expression, SCYL-1 regulates SLO-2 through physical interactions.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: The human Slo2.2/Slack is also regulated by SCYL1.
source: Importantly, we found that the human Slo2.2/Slack is also regulated by SCYL1.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recordings from Xenopus oocytes.

claim: The biological significance of RNA editing at non-coding regions is only beginning to be appreciated.
source: The biological significance of RNA editing at non-coding regions is only beginning to be appreciated.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field.

claim: A recent study with C. elegans identified many neuron-specific A-to-I editing sites in the 3'-UTR of clec-41.
source: A recent study with C. elegans identified many neuron-specific A-to-I editing sites in the 3'-UTR of clec-41, and showed that elimination of these editing events by adr-2 knockout compromises clec-41 expression and impairs a chemotaxis behavior (Deffit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Elimination of editing events in clec-41 by adr-2 knockout compromises clec-41 expression and impairs a chemotaxis behavior.
source: A recent study with C. elegans identified many neuron-specific A-to-I editing sites in the 3'-UTR of clec-41, and showed that elimination of these editing events by adr-2 knockout compromises clec-41 expression and impairs a chemotaxis behavior (Deffit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An A-to-I RNA editing event at the 3'UTR of scyl-1 controls its expression.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that an A-to-I RNA editing event at the 3'UTR of scyl-1 controls its expression, and that SCYL-1 contributes to neuronal whole-cell currents through a direct effect on SLO-2.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and reporter assays.

claim: SCYL-1 contributes to neuronal whole-cell currents through a direct effect on SLO-2.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that an A-to-I RNA editing event at the 3'UTR of scyl-1 controls its expression, and that SCYL-1 contributes to neuronal whole-cell currents through a direct effect on SLO-2.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and single-channel analysis.

claim: RNA editing at a single site in the 3'-UTR could have a profound effect on gene expression.
source: Our results demonstrate that RNA editing at a single site in the 3'-UTR could have a profound effect on gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assay results.

claim: The A-to-I conversion at the ADR-1-regulated editing site increases base pairing in the putative double-stranded structure of scyl-1 3'-UTR.
source: The A-to-I conversion at the ADR-1-regulated editing site increases base pairing in the putative double-stranded structure of scyl-1 3'-UTR (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is inferred from the predicted secondary structure shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Editing at the ADR-1-dependent site in scyl-1 3'-UTR is likely important to recruiting putative regulatory proteins to increase mRNA stability.
source: In combination with the observation that GFP signal was undetectable in transgenic worms expressing a reporter construct containing the non-edited scyl-1 3'-UTR, this result suggests that RNA editing at the ADR-1-dependent site in scyl-1 3'-UTR is likely important to recruiting the putative regulatory proteins to increase mRNA stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter assay and genetic screen results.

claim: scyl-1 has four different transcripts with identical 5'-UTR and coding sequence but different 3'-UTRs of variable lengths and sequences.
source: scyl-1 has four different transcripts with identical 5'-UTR and coding sequence but different 3'-UTRs of variable lengths (ranging from 167 to 1862 nucleotides) and sequences (www.wormbase.org).
evidence: This is based on information from WormBase.

claim: The ADR-1-dependent editing site exists only in the transcript with the longest 3'-UTR.
source: The ADR-1-dependent editing site exists only in the transcript with the longest 3'-UTR.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data and transcript structure.

claim: ADR-1 may regulate scyl-1 expression in a cell-specific manner depending on where the specific transcript is expressed.
source: The presence of an ADR-1-regulated editing site in this but not the other transcripts suggests that ADR-1 may regulate scyl-1 expression in a cell-specific manner depending on where the specific transcript is expressed.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the transcript structure.

claim: The 3'-UTR of human SCYL1 transcripts has a high probability of forming hair-pin structures based on software prediction.
source: Interestingly, the 3'-UTR of human SCYL1 transcripts (NM_020680.4) also has a high probability of forming hair-pin structures based on software prediction (https://rna.urmc.rochester.edu/RNAstructureWeb/Servers).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction.

claim: SCYL1 proteins are evolutionarily conserved proteins that share an N-terminal pseudokinase domain.
source: SCYL1 proteins are evolutionarily conserved proteins that share an N-terminal pseudokinase domain (Manning et al., 2002; Pelletier, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SCYL1 may regulate intracellular trafficking between the Golgi apparatus and the ER.
source: Results of previous studies with cultured cells suggest that SCYL1 may regulate intracellular trafficking between the Golgi apparatus and the ER (Burman et al., 2008; Burman et al., 2010), and facilitate nuclear tRNA export by acting at the nuclear pore complex (Chafe and Mangroo, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SCYL1 may facilitate nuclear tRNA export by acting at the nuclear pore complex.
source: Results of previous studies with cultured cells suggest that SCYL1 may regulate intracellular trafficking between the Golgi apparatus and the ER (Burman et al., 2008; Burman et al., 2010), and facilitate nuclear tRNA export by acting at the nuclear pore complex (Chafe and Mangroo, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutations of SCYL1 in humans are associated with a variety of disorders, including neurodegeneration, intellectual disabilities, and liver failure.
source: Mutations of SCYL1 in humans are associated with a variety of disorders, including neurodegeneration, intellectual disabilities, and liver failure (Lenz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Schmidt et al., 2015; Shohet et al., 2019; Spagnoli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: Mice with SCYL1 deficiency develop an early onset and progressive neurodegenerative disorder.
source: Mice with SCYL1 deficiency develop an early onset and progressive neurodegenerative disorder (Pelletier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: It is unclear whether the documented mutant phenotypes of SCYL1 are related to its roles in intracellular trafficking and nuclear tRNA export.
source: However, it is unclear whether the documented mutant phenotypes of SCYL1 are related to its roles in intracellular trafficking and nuclear tRNA export (Pelletier, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: This study brings into view a new potential mechanism for SCYL1 mutation-associated disorders: impairing Slo2 channel function.
source: This study brings into view a new potential mechanism for SCYL1 mutation-associated disorders: impairing Slo2 channel function.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: SCYL-1 likely regulates channel function either directly or through a closely associated protein.
source: Since SCYL-1 physically associates with SLO-2, and enhances SLO-2 single-channel Po by altering the open and closed states, it likely regulates channel function either directly or through a closely associated protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the physical interaction and functional data.

claim: The similar effects of SCYL-1 and SCYL1 on Slo2 channels suggest that they likely play an important role in Slo2 physiological functions across animal species.
source: Although the exact mechanism remains to be determined, the similar effects of SCYL-1 and SCYL1 on Slo2 channels suggest that they likely play an important role in Slo2 physiological functions across animal species.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the regulatory mechanism.

claim: The expression patterns of scyl-1 and slo-2 largely do not overlap.
source: The expression patterns of scyl-1 and slo-2 largely do not overlap.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data.

claim: The regulatory effect of SCYL-1 on SLO-2 is cell- and tissue-specific.
source: Although they are coexpressed in ventral cord motor neurons, most other neurons expressing slo-2 do not express scyl-1, suggesting that the regulatory effect of SCYL-1 on SLO-2 is cell- and tissue-specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern data.

claim: SCYL-1 physiological functions are not limited to regulating SLO-2.
source: The expression of scyl-1 in cells not expressing slo-2 suggests that SCYL-1 physiological functions are not limited to regulating SLO-2.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern data.

claim: In mouse, SCYL1 and Slo2.2 are both expressed in the hippocampus and cerebellum but their expression patterns do not completely overlap.
source: In mouse, SCYL1 and Slo2.2 are both expressed in the hippocampus and cerebellum but their expression patterns do not completely overlap (Joiner et al., 1998; Schmidt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The regulation of hSlo2.2 by SCYL1 might occur in a cell- and tissue-specific manner.
source: Conceivably, the regulation of hSlo2.2 by SCYL1 might also occur in a cell- and tissue-specific manner, and SCYL1 likely performs other physiological functions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the expression patterns.

claim: SCYL1 likely performs other physiological functions beyond regulating Slo2.2.
source: Conceivably, the regulation of hSlo2.2 by SCYL1 might also occur in a cell- and tissue-specific manner, and SCYL1 likely performs other physiological functions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference.

claim: The pleiotropic phenotypes observed in patients and mice with SCYL1 mutations support the possibility that SCYL1 performs other physiological functions.
source: The latter possibility is supported by the pleiotropic phenotypes observed in patients and mice with SCYL1 mutations (Lenz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Pelletier et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2015; Shohet et al., 2019; Spagnoli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical and animal studies.

claim: ADAR-mediated RNA editing controls the expression of SCYL-1.
source: In summary, this study demonstrates that ADAR-mediated RNA editing controls the expression of SCYL-1, which interacts with SLO-2 to allow SLO-2 perform its physiological functions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: SCYL-1 interacts with SLO-2 to allow SLO-2 perform its physiological functions.
source: In summary, this study demonstrates that ADAR-mediated RNA editing controls the expression of SCYL-1, which interacts with SLO-2 to allow SLO-2 perform its physiological functions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This regulatory mechanism is conserved with mammalian SCYL1 and Slo2.
source: Moreover, this study shows that this regulatory mechanism is conserved with mammalian SCYL1 and Slo2.
evidence: This is supported by the experiments with human Slo2.2 and mouse SCYL1.

claim: The findings reveal a new molecular mechanism of Slo2 channel regulation.
source: Our findings reveal a new molecular mechanism of Slo2 channel regulation, and provide the bases for investigating how physiological functions of human Slo2 are regulated by SCYL1, and whether the neurodegeneration and intellectual disability phenotypes of SCYL1 mutations are related to Slo2 channel dysfunction.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contributions.
